731.event_title: Emperor Zhenzong distributes drought-resistant Champa rice
731.place: Lower Yangtze and Huai river regions, Song China
731.event: After a severe drought struck the lower Yangtze and Huai river valleys in 1012, the Song emperor Zhenzong had thirty thousand bushels of early-ripening, drought-resistant rice seed from Champa, in present-day central Vietnam, distributed to farmers in the stricken areas. He also had instructions on how to grow the new rice circulated to the farmers. The fast-maturing variety could be grown on higher ground and, in many places, allowed two harvests a year.
731.explanation: The new rice made harvests far less vulnerable to drought, and historians link its spread to the growth of population in southern China.
731.tie_back: The kural names harvests that never fail as the first mark of a true country, and Zhenzong's distribution of Champa rice was a deliberate effort to make his land's harvests failure-proof.
731._accuracy_note: Illustrates only the first of the kural's three marks, unfailing harvests; the worthy people and prosperous merchants are not part of this story.

732.event_title: Augustus annexes Egypt and makes it Rome's granary
732.event: After defeating Mark Antony and Cleopatra, Octavian, later called Augustus, arrived in Egypt in 30 BCE, ended the Ptolemaic monarchy and annexed the country as his personal domain, governed by a prefect of his choosing. Egypt's wealth was largely agricultural, and its grain supplied the city of Rome; its revenues were almost equal to those of Gaul. Historians count the addition of Egypt as a major supplier of the capital among Augustus's most important measures for Rome's food supply.
732.explanation: Egypt's dependable Nile harvests made it so valuable that Rome's ruler kept it under his own direct control.
732.tie_back: The kural describes a true country as one so rich that others desire it, free of ruinous calamities and yielding abundant harvests, and Egypt was coveted and seized by Rome for exactly that wealth.
732._accuracy_note: A strong fit for a land coveted for its abundant harvests; the 'free from calamity' element is implied by Egypt's reliability rather than documented here.

733.event_title: The Edict of Potsdam opens Brandenburg to Huguenot refugees
733.event: After Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes, which had protected French Protestants, Elector Frederick William of Brandenburg issued the Edict of Potsdam offering the Huguenots refuge. It promised help with travel, free choice of where to settle, houses and building materials, tax exemptions, the right to practise their trades and their own French-language churches. At least 20,000 Huguenots settled in his lands, which had been thinned by the Thirty Years' War.
733.explanation: A land with resources to spare took in a sudden wave of refugees and turned them into farmers, artisans and manufacturers who strengthened the state.
733.tie_back: The kural praises the country that can bear a heavy burden that falls on it all at once, which Parimelazhagar explains as people fleeing from neighbouring lands, and Brandenburg's welcome of the Huguenots is a classic example.
733._accuracy_note: Closely matches the commentators' reading of absorbing refugees; the kural's second point, still paying the ruler his full dues, is reversed here by the generous tax exemptions.

734.event_title: War, crowding and plague strike Athens
734.event: Early in the Peloponnesian War, Pericles allowed the people of the Attic countryside to take refuge inside the walls of Athens while the Spartans raided the land, and the city became severely overcrowded. In 430 BCE a plague broke out in the crowded city and over the following years killed a large part of its population, including both of Pericles' legitimate sons. When the Spartans again invaded and laid waste to the fields in 429 BCE, crops could not be planted, and Pericles himself died of the plague that autumn.
734.explanation: Athens, the richest city in Greece, was brought low when a destructive enemy, hunger and an unrelenting epidemic struck together.
734.tie_back: The kural says a true country is one untouched by crushing hunger, endless disease and destructive enemies, and Athens in 430 to 429 BCE shows what befalls a land when all three arrive at once.
734._accuracy_note: A negative illustration that matches the kural's triad of hunger, disease and enemies very closely.

735.event: A group of conspirators led by Robert Catesby planned to blow up the House of Lords during the State Opening of Parliament, killing King James I, his family, his chief ministers and the members present. An anonymous letter warned Lord Monteagle to stay away from Parliament, and he passed it to the government. On the night of 4 November 1605 a search of the cellars beneath the House of Lords found Guy Fawkes with 36 barrels of gunpowder, and the plot collapsed.
735.explanation: The plot showed how a small band of internal enemies could threaten to destroy a kingdom's entire leadership in a single stroke.
735.tie_back: The kural says a true country is free of internal enemies who work ruin and of murderous bands that trouble the ruler, and the Gunpowder Plot is one of history's best-known examples of exactly such a danger.
735._accuracy_note: A clear negative illustration of an internal plot against the ruler; the kural's warning about rival factions in general is only partly reflected.

736.event_title: Tokyo is rebuilt after the Great Kanto Earthquake
736.event: On 1 September 1923 a magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck the Kanto region, and the fires that followed destroyed much of Tokyo. Within weeks the government set up the Imperial Capital Reconstruction Department under Home Minister Goto Shinpei to plan the city's recovery. Over the following years land readjustment and the rebuilding of streets, bridges, canals and parks were carried out across the burned districts, laying the foundations of modern Tokyo.
736.explanation: Even after one of the worst disasters of the century, Japan had the resources and organisation to rebuild its capital on a better plan.
736.tie_back: The kural praises the land that, even when ruin comes, does not lose its richness, and the reconstruction of Tokyo after 1923 shows a country recovering its strength after catastrophe.
736._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of resilience after ruin, though the reconstruction was scaled back from Goto's original plan for lack of funds.

737.event_title: King Kassapa I builds his capital on the rock of Sigiriya
737.event: King Kassapa I made Sigiriya his capital, building a palace on the summit of a granite rock that rises about 180 metres above the surrounding plain and intending it as a safeguard against his enemies. Visitors entered through a gigantic brick and plaster lion whose paws still frame the stairway. At the foot of the rock lay elaborate water gardens with ponds and terraces, surrounded by a moat.
737.explanation: Sigiriya combined a natural rock fortress, carefully managed water and surrounding lands into a single royal stronghold that is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.
737.tie_back: The kural lists water, well-placed hills and a strong fortress as the limbs of a country, and Sigiriya, a hill fortress ringed by water gardens and a moat, brings these features together in one place.
737._accuracy_note: Shows hill, water and fortress combined, but at the scale of a single royal site rather than a whole country, and Kassapa lost his throne in 495 despite it.

738.event_title: The first Human Development Report introduces the Human Development Index
738.place: United Nations Development Programme, New York, United States
738.event: In 1990 the UN Development Programme published the first Human Development Report, led by the economist Mahbub ul Haq with Amartya Sen as a key collaborator. It introduced the Human Development Index, which ranks countries not by income alone but by an average of longevity, education and standard of living. The report argued that development should be judged by whether people can lead long, healthy and creative lives.
738.explanation: The index changed how the world measures national success, treating health and knowledge as being as important as wealth.
738.tie_back: The kural names freedom from disease, wealth, good harvests, happiness and security as the ornaments of a country, and the Human Development Index similarly judges nations by health and well-being as well as wealth.
738._accuracy_note: A reasonable parallel in spirit; the index's components overlap with only some of the kural's five ornaments, and security is not among them.

739.event_title: Oil is struck at Burgan, Kuwait
739.event: Surface seepages of bitumen at Burgan had long hinted at oil, and in 1934 the ruler of Kuwait granted a concession to the Kuwait Oil Company, a joint venture of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company and Gulf Oil. Burgan No. 1, drilled at a seepage beginning in 1936, struck a high-pressure oil-bearing sandstone in February 1938. Exports began in 1946, and the Great Burgan field became one of the largest in the world, the main source of Kuwait's wealth.
739.explanation: A small country's prosperity came above all from the riches already lying beneath its soil.
739.tie_back: The kural honours lands whose wealth comes from their natural endowment rather than from endless toil, and Kuwait's fortune from the Burgan field is a modern example of riches given by the land itself.
739._accuracy_note: Next-best fit: the wealth was a natural endowment, but it still had to be sought through years of exploration and drilling, which the kural contrasts with true natural plenty.

740.event_title: The reign of Charles II, last Habsburg king of Spain
740.event: Charles II inherited the vast Spanish empire at the age of four in 1665. Chronically ill and widely regarded as unable to govern effectively, he was dominated by court factions while Spain suffered economic troubles and military setbacks against Louis XIV. He fathered no children, and the dispute over his succession after his death in 1700 led to the War of the Spanish Succession and the break-up of Spain's European possessions.
740.explanation: Spain still ruled one of the largest empires in the world, but without a capable ruler its great resources could not prevent decline.
740.tie_back: The kural says that even a land with every good quality bears no fruit without a fitting ruler, and Spain under Charles II is a well-known case of vast wealth undone by a king unable to rule.
740._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of riches without effective rule, though historians note that many of Spain's problems predated his reign.
